changes.reason: The second clause still hangs on quomodo (“how … corruisti in terram”), a lament parallel to “How have you fallen,” not a yes-or-no question as “Have you collapsed” makes it.

changes.before: Judah's covering will be exposed, and on that day you will look to the armory of the House of the Forest.
changes.after: Judah's covering will be exposed, and on that day you will see the armory of the House of the Forest.
changes.reason: The Vulgate has simply videbis armamentarium (“you will see the armory”); “look to” adds a sense of relying on it that the Latin does not carry.

changes.before: He will wind you round and round with affliction; He will throw you like a ball into a broad and spacious land. There you will die, and there will be your glorious chariot, you disgrace to your master's house.
changes.after: He will crown you with a crown of affliction; He will throw you like a ball into a broad and spacious land. There you will die, and there will be your glorious chariot, you disgrace to your master's house.
changes.reason: Coronas coronabit te tribulatione is the Vulgate’s image of a crown of tribulation (as in the Douay); “wind you round and round” renders the Hebrew, not the Latin.

changes.before: Bring your case forward, says the Lord; present anything strong that you have, says the King of Jacob.
changes.after: Bring your case forward, says the Lord; present anything you may have, says the King of Jacob.
changes.reason: In si quid forte habetis, forte is the adverb “perhaps” (Douay “if perhaps you have any thing”), not fortis “strong”; “anything strong” imports the Hebrew’s “strong arguments” reading.

changes.before: Look, they have become like stubble; fire has burned them. They will not deliver themselves from the power of the flame. These are no coals for warming themselves, no hearth to sit beside.
changes.after: Look, they have become like stubble; fire has burned them. They will not deliver themselves from the power of the flame. There are no coals to warm them, no hearth to sit beside.
changes.reason: Non sunt prunæ quibus calefiant says there will be no coals for them to warm themselves at; “These are no coals” follows the Hebrew image of the consuming fire rather than the Latin.

changes.before: You neither heard nor knew, nor was your ear opened long ago. For I know that you will act treacherously, and I have called you a transgressor from the womb.
changes.after: You neither heard nor knew, nor was your ear opened long ago. For I know that you will surely act treacherously, and I have called you a transgressor from the womb.
changes.reason: Prævaricans prævaricaberis doubles the verb for emphasis (Douay “transgressing thou wilt transgress”); the plain “you will act treacherously” drops it, unlike “Gaudens gaudebo” in 61:10, which the column renders “greatly rejoice”.

changes.before: For who will pity you, Jerusalem, or grieve for you? Who will go to ask about your welfare?
changes.after: For who will pity you, Jerusalem, or grieve for you? Who will go to plead for your peace?
changes.reason: Ad rogandum pro pace tua means going to entreat on behalf of Jerusalem’s peace (Douay “to pray for thy peace”), not to inquire after her welfare, which is the Hebrew idiom rather than the Vulgate’s.

changes.before: “Therefore, look, this time I will make them know; I will show them My hand and My might, and they will know that My name is the Lord.”
changes.after: “Therefore, look, this time I will show them; I will show them My hand and My might, and they will know that My name is the Lord.”
changes.reason: The Latin deliberately repeats ostendam eis (“I will show them this time, I will show them My hand”), and “make them know” both loses that repetition and anticipates the closing et scient.

changes.before: Thus says the Lord: “Go and obtain a potter's earthenware jar from the elders of the people and the elders of the priests.
changes.after: Thus says the Lord: “Go and get a potter's earthenware jar, and take with you some of the elders of the people and some of the elders of the priests.
changes.reason: A senioribus populi is partitive (Douay “take of the ancients of the people”): the elders are the men who go with Jeremiah in 19:10, whereas “obtain a jar from the elders” makes them the source of the jar.

changes.before: But like the very bad figs, too bad to eat, thus says the Lord: So will I make Zedekiah king of Judah, his rulers, and the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this city and those who live in the land of Egypt.
changes.after: But like the very bad figs, too bad to eat, thus says the Lord: So will I give up Zedekiah king of Judah, his rulers, and the remnant of Jerusalem who remain in this city and those who live in the land of Egypt.
changes.reason: Sic dabo Sedeciam means “so will I give up Zedekiah” (Douay “so will I give Sedecias”); “make Zedekiah king of Judah” with no complement sounds aloud as if God were making him king.

changes.before: For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Take from My hand this cup of the wine of fury, and give it to all the nations to whom I send you to drink.
changes.after: For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Take from My hand this cup of the wine of fury, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it.
changes.reason: Propinabis de illo cunctis gentibus means giving the nations a drink from the cup; “to whom I send you to drink” sounds aloud as if the prophet is sent to drink.

changes.before: I took the cup from the Lord's hand and gave it to all the nations to whom the Lord sent me to drink:
changes.after: I took the cup from the Lord's hand and made all the nations to whom the Lord sent me drink from it:
changes.reason: Propinavi cunctis gentibus means “I gave all the nations to drink”; “sent me to drink” misleads the ear, and the wording now matches the command in 32:15.

changes.before: the prophets who were before me and before you from the beginning prophesied against many lands and great kingdoms of war, affliction, and famine.
changes.after: the prophets who were before me and before you from the beginning prophesied of war, affliction, and famine against many lands and great kingdoms.
changes.reason: De prælio, et de afflictione, et de fame is what the prophets foretold; placed after “kingdoms”, “great kingdoms of war” sounds like a description of the kingdoms.

changes.before: “Thus says the Lord: We have heard a cry of terror, fear, and no peace.
changes.after: “Thus says the Lord: We have heard a cry of terror; there is dread, and no peace.
changes.reason: Vocem terroris audivimus: formido, et non est pax makes formido a separate statement (there is dread), but the current line lists “fear” and “no peace” as things heard, which does not parse aloud.

changes.before: You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of fathers into the laps of their children after them. Most strong, great, and mighty, Your name is the Lord of hosts.
changes.after: You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of fathers into the laps of their children after them. O most strong, great, and mighty One, Your name is the Lord of hosts.
changes.reason: Fortissime, magne, et potens are vocatives addressed to God; read aloud, “Most strong, great, and mighty, Your name…” sounds as if the adjectives describe the name.

changes.before: Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the fighting men, and all the people did not obey the voice of the Lord by remaining in the land of Judah.
changes.after: Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the fighting men, and all the people did not obey the voice of the Lord to remain in the land of Judah.
changes.reason: Ut manerent in terra Juda is what the Lord commanded (to remain); “did not obey … by remaining” can be heard as saying that remaining was the disobedience.

changes.before: A continual allowance of food was given him by the king of Babylon, a daily portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
changes.after: His allowance of food, a continual allowance, was given him by the king of Babylon, a daily portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
changes.reason: The Latin deliberately repeats cibaria ejus, cibaria perpetua (his provisions, continual provisions), which the current line collapses into one phrase.

changes.before: Their legs were straight legs, and the sole of each foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot, with sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze.
changes.after: Their feet were straight feet, and the sole of each foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot, with sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze.
changes.reason: The Vulgate has pedes eorum, pedes recti (“their feet were straight feet”), and “legs” follows the Hebrew raglayim rather than the Latin, which then speaks of the sole of the foot.

changes.before: As for you, son of man, look, they will put bonds on you and bind you with them, and you will not go out from among them.
changes.after: As for you, son of man, look, bonds have been put upon you, and they will bind you with them, and you will not go out from among them.
changes.reason: Ecce data sunt super te vincula is perfect passive (“bonds have been put upon you”), followed by the future ligabunt; the English turned the completed fact into a future act.

changes.before: I, the Lord, have spoken. When I send the deadly arrows of famine against them, arrows that bring death, which I will send to destroy you, I will heap famine upon you and break the staff of bread among you.
changes.after: I, the Lord, have spoken. When I send the evil arrows of famine against them, arrows that bring death, which I will send to destroy you, I will heap famine upon you and break the staff of bread among you.
changes.reason: Sagittas famis pessimas are “most evil” arrows, and mortiferæ (“that bring death”) follows separately; “deadly … that bring death” drops pessimas and says the same thing twice.
